To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

congenitally blind individuals can use a tongue-based sensory substitution device to perform a visual discrimination task, and that this cross modal plasticability can be observed using brain imaging.

(1) the visual cortex of congenitally and early blind subjects can be activated by stimulation of the tongue, and (2) that this cross modal plastic response can be induced by a 1 week training period.
congenitally blind individuals develop a visual-like cortical representation after training to use a tongue-based sensory substitution device.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the plasticity of the human visual cortex in congenital blindness and its relation to the use of sensory substitution.
how the brain adapts to sensory deprivation.
the development and application of new sensory substitution technologies for blind people.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the visual cortex of congenitally sighted subjects is able to respond to tactile input after training with a sensory substitution device, the TDU.
the brain of the blind subjects has learned to use the tongue as a substitute for vision, and that this learning is reflected in the occipital activation.
the visual cortex of congenitally blinded subjects can be activated by somatosensory input, but not by visual stimulation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that the visual cortex of congenitally and early blind subjects is not silent, but is capable of being activated through the somatosensery system.

the visual cortex can be reprogrammed by intensive training with sensory substitution devices, and that the visual cortex of blind subjects may be more malleable to cross modal plasticity than that of sighted individuals.
cross modal plasticity can be used as a tool for rehabilitation in the blind.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the visual cortex of the blind is not necessarily a dead tissue and that the plasticity of the brain can be exploited to restore sensory function.
cross modal plasticity is possible even in the absence of vision during the critical period of brain development.
sensory substitution is a promising approach to help people who are blind to regain visual perception and to learn new visual skills.
